extracted.intended_audience: writers, playwrights, and scholars/theorists of comedy and humor
extracted.subtask_description: Theory-and-practice guidance for producing comic effects and comic character-types on stage or in writing, explaining what makes things laughable and how to observe, construct and deploy types. Useful for playwrights, comedy writers and students of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy depicts general types (object of high-class comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus, to depict characters, that is to say, general types, is the object of high-class comedy.” Comedy’s essential aim is to give general types rather than unique individuals; it is the one art that aims at the general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with tragedy and other arts (which aim at the individual). Use titles and labeling that emphasize classes (examples: Le Misanthrope, L'Avare, Le Joueur, Le Distrait). When composing, aim to reveal a type that will be recognisable beyond a single person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of comic observation: external, generalising, inductive
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic observation is directed outwards, settling on the surface and producing general results: 'observation is always external and the result always general.' The comic proceeds by comparing analogous cases and extracting an essence or ‘average’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt deep psychological penetration of individuality when you want to create comic effect; favor external traits, repeated patterns and features that allow abstraction into a category (the same method as inductive sciences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of an ideal comic type
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideally comic type 'must be deep-rooted, so as to supply comedy with inexhaustible matter, and yet superficial, in order that it may remain within the scope of comedy; invisible to its actual owner ... visible to everybody else ... extremely considerate to its own self ... troublesome to others ... immediately repressible ... sure of reappearing ... inseparable from social life ... capable ... of being tacked on to all the vices and even to a good many virtues.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing a comic type, try to combine these attributes so the trait (1) recurs, (2) is socially situated, (3) is unconscious to the owner, (4) provokes others to corrective action, and (5) can appear in many guises (attached to different virtues/vices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconsciousness of the fault (invisibility to its owner)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic 'partakes of the unconscious' and the laughable trait is 'invisible to its actual owner, but visible to everybody else.' Laughter presupposes that the subject does not perceive their own ludicrous feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the ridiculous quality something the character cannot or does not see in themselves—this preserves the social, corrective function of laughter and enables general laughter from the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity as a central source of the laughable
rubrics_metrics.description: Vanity is singled out as the widespread mixture that supplies comic matter: 'This mixture is vanity ... the one failing that is essentially laughable is vanity.' Vanity is at once superficial and deep-rooted, and draws many other faults into its orbit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for manifestations of vanity (self-admiration, exaggerated self-importance, dependence on imagined admiration) as a frequent, productive source of comic situations and characters; laughter functions to neutralise vanity socially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as social corrective: convert rigidity into plasticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter’s function is to repress separatist tendencies and readapt the individual to the whole: 'Its function is to convert rigidity into plasticity, to readapt the individual to the whole, in short, to round off the corners wherever they are met with.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame comic situations so that ridicule points to a social maladjustment and invites corrective reaction—comedy should aim at social reintegration rather than merely malicious derision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional comic (professional vanity, solemnity, callousness, jargon, professional logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professions create ready-made categories and comic varieties: professional vanity (exalting one’s art), solemnity (treating the public as made for the profession), professional callousness, confinement to professional jargon, and a 'professional logic' that is valid within a circle but comic outside it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit occupational habits, technical jargon and locally valid reasoning as comic tools—show practitioners applying their specialised language or logic to ordinary life to expose absurdity. Examples: Molière’s doctors, Regnard’s Joueur, Labiche’s timber-merchant character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple instances/satellites to establish a type
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic poet tends 'to cause other characters, displaying the same general traits, to revolve as satellites round him'—showing several copies of a model helps define a species (as the naturalist does).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, present several characters who share the trait so the audience perceives it as a type rather than a one-off quirk; group or collective titles (Les Femmes savantes, Les Précieuses ridicules) emphasize this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific kind of absurdity (comic logic) rather than general absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic absurdity is a particular kind of contradiction tied to its cause: 'absurdity, when met with in the comic, is not absurdity IN GENERAL ... It is an absurdity of a definite kind.' The comic infuses absurdity with its own particular essence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid generic 'absurd' situations; find the specific mismatch between social function, habit, or privileged idea and the present reality (e.g., Don Quixote’s romances creating a privileged recollection that forces a misperception). The comic arises from that specific, causally-grounded incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words and speech promote generality (language tends to generalise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words (except proper nouns) 'all denote genera' and thus intervene between things and ourselves, tending to conceal individuality and to encourage perception of types and generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that language itself encourages typification—use labels, stock phrases, and generic expressions to compress individuality into a recognisable comic type, or conversely, exploit the gap between label and individual for comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic elements migrate: subtleness can yield coarse comic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher/subtler comic elements (e.g., vanity) can slide down into coarse comic effects; 'many coarse comic effects are the direct result of a drop from some very subtle comic element.' Examples: disproportion in partners (short man/very tall) read as an attempt to 'raise himself' like the frog and ox.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace the lineage of a comic impression—what begins as a subtle psychological trait can produce broad physical or situational comedy. Use this transposition deliberately to escalate or simplify comic effects for different audiences.
